# Mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic in a longitudinal study of Hurricane Katrina survivors

**Authors:** Meghan Zacher; Ethan J Raker; Marie-Claire Meadows; Saúl Ramírez; Tyler Woods; Sarah R Lowe

**Affiliations:** aPopulation Studies and Training Center, Brown University, Providence, RI, 02912, USA | bDepartment of Sociology, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada | cDepartment of Chronic Disease Epidemiology, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, 06510, USA | dDepartment of Sociology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, 02138, USA | eDepartment of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, 06510, USA

## Abstract

While the COVID-19 pandemic is known to have caused widespread mental health challenges, it remains unknown how the prevalence, presentation, and predictors of mental health adversity during the pandemic compare to other mass crises. We shed light on this question using longitudinal survey data (2003–2021) from 424 low-income mothers who were affected by both the pandemic and Hurricane Katrina, which struck the U.S. Gulf Coast in 2005. The prevalence of elevated posttraumatic stress symptoms was similar 1-year into the pandemic (41.6%) as 1-year post-Katrina (41.9%), while elevated psychological distress was more prevalent 1-year into the pandemic (48.3%) than 1-year post-Katrina (37.2%). Adjusted logistic regression models showed that pandemic-related bereavement, fear or worry, lapsed medical care, and economic stressors predicted mental health adversity during the pandemic. Similar exposures were associated with mental health adversity post-Katrina. Findings underscore the continued need for pandemic-related mental health services and suggest that preventing traumatic or stressful exposures may reduce the mental health impacts of future mass crises.

Keywords: COVID-19 pandemic, Hurricane Katrina, Disasters, Mental health, Posttraumatic stress, Psychological distress

## Introduction

As the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic emerged, scholars and practitioners urged officials to prepare for surging mental health needs by drawing parallels to previous mass crises (Esterwood and Saeed, 2020; Galea et al., 2020; Raker et al., 2020), the mental health consequences of which are well-documented (Goldmann and Galea, 2014). As anticipated, mental health needs rose during the pandemic and have been linked to stressors that disproportionately burdened marginalized groups (Bertoldo et al., 2022; Ettman et al., 2020; Perry et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021). Yet, while reflections on prior events helped raise alarms about mental health in the COVID-19 era, it remains unknown how the prevalence, presentation, and predictors of mental health adversity during the pandemic compare to other mass crises.

Differences between pandemics and other mass crises could render their psychological impacts incomparable. The COVID-19 pandemic has been more geographically and temporally diffuse and may be less likely to cause trauma than prior disasters (Ng et al., 2020). Traumatic exposures are defined in the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) as experiencing or witnessing “actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence,” learning of such an event occurring to a family member or close friend, or being repeatedly and directly exposed to details of traumatic incidents (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Many common pandemic-related experiences, such as minor illness, persistent worry, and disruptions to healthcare, childcare, and employment, may not be considered traumatic under these guidelines. Distinguishing trauma from nontraumatic stressors is not simply semantic. Traumatic experiences may prompt symptoms of posttraumatic stress (PTS) and are required for diagnosing PTS disorder, whereas nontraumatic stressors may instead cause depression, anxiety, and generalized psychological distress (PD). That said, debates surrounding the definition of trauma and diagnosis of PTS disorder are longstanding and have been reinvigorated by the pandemic (Horesh and Brown, 2020; McNally, 2003; Norrholm et al., 2021). Ultimately, it remains unknown which experiences in particular—traumatic or not—were associated with PTS symptoms and other mental health challenges during the pandemic and how they compare to predictors of adversity following other events.

Comparing mental health adversity during the COVID-19 pandemic to other disasters will assist practitioners treating pandemic-related symptoms and inform responses to future mass crises. Unfortunately, such comparisons are complicated by data limitations. Because disaster studies often evaluate outcomes following singular, localized events, the populations sampled and the measures gathered vary. This makes it difficult to discern whether differences in mental health outcomes result from distinct event typology, characteristics of the affected populations, or measurements. Relatedly, few studies can account for pre-existing resources and vulnerabilities that may influence psychopathology, including prior mental health and disaster exposure (Goldmann and Galea, 2014).

The current study addressed these issues using longitudinal survey data from 424 women who experienced both the COVID-19 pandemic and Hurricane Katrina, which devastated the Gulf Coast of the United States in 2005. The sample included primarily Black, low-income mothers, a demographic subgroup that has been disproportionately affected by the pandemic and prior disasters (Clouston et al., 2021; Cooper and Williams, 2020; Goldmann and Galea, 2014). Drawing on five surveys conducted between 2003 and 2021, we compared respondents’ mental health during the pandemic to their mental health before and after Hurricane Katrina, assessing symptoms of PTS and PD. Then, we examined which of 14 pandemic-related exposures predicted mental health adversity during the pandemic, controlling for pre-pandemic characteristics and vulnerabilities. In the Discussion, we consider our results alongside those of a previous study, which found that experiencing bereavement, fear or worry, and difficulty accessing medical care predicted mental health adversity after Hurricane Katrina (Raker et al., 2020).

## Methods

### Data and sample

We used data from the Resilience in Survivors of Katrina (RISK) project. RISK originated in 2003 as Opening Doors, an intervention to improve retention at community colleges. Students at two New Orleans-area schools were eligible if they were parents aged 18 to 34 earning less than 200% of the federal poverty line. Recruitment efforts yielded a sample of 1019 low-income parents, 943 (92.5%) of whom were mothers. Eligibility for follow-up surveys and for the current study was restricted to the 943 mothers. Baseline (BL) surveys were conducted between November 2003 and February 2005, approximately 1-year pre-Katrina. Hurricane Katrina disrupted Opening Doors in August 2005, and the RISK project took over. Four post-Katrina follow-up surveys have since been conducted: (F1) March 2006–March 2007, about 1-year post-Katrina (n ​= ​668 women; response rate [RR] ​= ​70.8% of the 943 eligible women); (F2) March 2009–April 2010, 4 years post-Katrina (n ​= ​703, RR ​= ​74.6%); (F3) November 2016–December 2018, 12 years post-Katrina (n ​= ​716, RR ​= ​75.9%); and (F4) February–November 2021, 16 years post-Katrina and 1-year into the COVID-19 pandemic, for which recruitment efforts focused on women who responded to F3 (n ​= ​430, RR ​= ​60.1% of 716 eligible women). Participants provided informed consent at each survey. The analytic sample for the current study included the 424 mothers who participated in F4 and had non-missing mental health measures at F4. Analyses also used data from BL, F1, F2, and F3. Missing data were multiply imputed across 20 chained imputations.

We evaluated the potential impact of selective attrition in two ways. First, we conducted two-sample t-tests and chi-square tests comparing the BL sociodemographic and health characteristics of women in our sample to those excluded. These analyses revealed no differences (all p ​> ​.05). Second, in sensitivity analyses presented in the Online Supplement, we re-estimated our main regression models accounting for selective attrition by applying inverse probability weights (Weuve et al., 2012). Results were substantively unchanged (Supplementary Tables S3 and S4).

### Measures

Mental Health Outcomes. We assessed hurricane- and pandemic-related PTS using the Impact of Event Scale-6 (IES-6) (Thoresen et al., 2010). In all post-Katrina surveys, respondents reported the extent to which they experienced six symptoms in the past seven days due to Hurricane Katrina, from 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely) (e.g., Other things kept making me think about it; I felt watchful and on-guard). At F4, respondents also completed the IES-6 questionnaire for symptoms related to the COVID-19 pandemic. We calculated the mean of the items (range: 0–4) and then dichotomized, coding scores 1.75 and higher “1” for elevated PTS symptoms (Hosey et al., 2019).

We assessed PD at all surveys with the Kessler-6 (K6) scale (Kessler et al., 2002). Respondents reported how often they felt six symptoms of distress (e.g., nervous; everything was an effort) in the past 30 days, from 0 (none of the time) to 4 (all of the time). We summed for scores ranging from 0 to 24. We then dichotomized with scores 8 and higher coded “1” for elevated PD symptoms (Furukawa et al., 2003). We also created a dichotomous measure of serious mental illness (scores 13+) (Kessler et al., 2003).

Pandemic-Related Exposures. We evaluated 14 pandemic-related exposures, all self-reported. Five exposures reflected personal experiences with COVID-19: The respondent had or probably had COVID-19; The respondent was seriously ill or hospitalized due to COVID-19; A relative or close friend had COVID-19; A relative or close friend was seriously ill or hospitalized due to COVID-19; A relative or close friend died from COVID-19. Two indicated fear or worry: The respondent was very or extremely worried that they may become seriously ill or die due to COVID-19; The respondent was very or extremely worried that a relative or close friend may become seriously ill or die due to COVID-19. The remaining measures reflected disruptions to healthcare, childcare, and household finances, indicating that since the pandemic began: The respondent was unable to access the medications they needed; The respondent had to delay medical care or was unable to access care when needed; Someone in the respondent’s household had unmet medical needs; The respondent became more involved in their children’s schooling; The respondent lost their job; The respondent’s household income declined; The respondent’s family did not have enough to eat. We also created an index reflecting the number of pandemic-related exposures reported.

Covariates. Models controlled for F4 survey month, age, self-reported race/ethnicity (non-Hispanic Black versus other), marital status (married or cohabiting versus neither), and the number of children living at home. We also controlled for pre-pandemic (F3) resources and vulnerabilities, including self-reported household income (less than $25,000; $25,000–49,000; and $50,000 or more), perceived social support, and mental and physical health. Social support was a continuous variable assessed using the Social Provisions Scale and ranging from 1 (low) to 4 (high) (Cutrona and Russell, 1987). We measured pre-pandemic mental health with PD and physical health with self-rated health (SRH) and physical symptoms. PD and SRH were linear covariates, with PD ranging from 0 to 24 and SRH from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). We measured physical symptoms with a binary variable indicating that the respondent experienced frequent migraines or headaches, back problems, or digestive problems in the past year. In addition, we controlled for an index of physical health conditions at F4: obesity, asthma, high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, and diabetes. Finally, we controlled for an index of twelve Hurricane Katrina-related exposures (e.g., was bereaved; feared life was in danger; could not access medical care; did not have enough food or water), which has been described elsewhere (Raker et al., 2020), as prior traumatic or stressful life events may predict mental health following subsequent exposures (Goldmann and Galea, 2014).

### Analysis

First, we examined descriptive statistics. Next, we calculated the percentage of respondents with elevated event-specific PTS and generalized PD symptoms across the five survey waves, restricting to respondents with non-missing data on PTS (n ​= ​296) and PD (n ​= ​290), respectively, in all waves. We evaluated whether prevalences differed significantly across waves using paired t-tests. Finally, we fit logistic regression models of elevated pandemic-related PTS and PD symptoms at F4 on individual pandemic-related exposures and the index. We estimated separate models for each of the 14 exposures and the index, rather than incorporating all variables in a single model, due to concerns over multicollinearity. All models controlled for sociodemographics, pre-pandemic resources and vulnerabilities, current physical conditions, and the Katrina-related exposure index. To facilitate comparisons, we report both estimated odds ratios (OR) and the average marginal effects (ME) of each exposure on the probability of elevated pandemic-related PTS and PD at F4. We consider p-values below .05 to be statistically significant, and we report 95% confidence intervals (CI), where appropriate, throughout.

## Results

Table 1 presents descriptive statistics. The average age was 25.3 (standard deviation [SD] ​= ​4.4) at BL and 42.1 (SD ​= ​4.4) at F4. All respondents were women, 84.1% were Black, 45.7% were married or cohabiting, and they had on average 1.5 (SD ​= ​1.3) children in the home at F4. Nearly all pandemic-related stressors were pervasive, affecting one in five respondents or more. On average, respondents experienced 4.6 (SD ​= ​2.7) of the 14 exposures.

Fig. 1 plots the percentage of respondents with elevated PTS and PD symptoms across survey waves. The prevalence of pandemic-related PTS at F4, 1-year into the pandemic (41.6%), was similar to that of hurricane-related PTS at F1, 1-year post-Katrina (41.9%, p ​= ​.926), and significantly higher than that of hurricane-related PTS at later waves (all p ​< ​.01). The percentage of respondents with elevated PD was significantly higher during the pandemic (F4, 48.3%) than any earlier wave (all p ​< ​.01), including F1, 1-year post-Katrina (37.2%, p ​= ​.004). The prevalence of serious mental illness was also higher at F4 (19.7%) than any earlier wave (all p ​< ​.01), including F1 (12.1%, p ​= ​.006).

BL = Baseline; F = Follow-up; PD = Psychological distress; PTS = Posttraumatic stress. 95% confidence intervals shown.*

Fig. 2 depicts the marginal effects of the 14 pandemic-related exposures on the probabilities of elevated pandemic-related PTS and PD at F4 from adjusted logistic regression models. Corresponding numeric results are presented in Supplementary Table S1 (odds ratios) and Supplementary Table S2 (marginal effects). Seven exposures were significantly associated with the probability of elevated PTS: having a relative or friend who was seriously ill due to COVID-19 (ME ​= ​0.099, CI ​= ​0.011, 0.188), being bereaved due to COVID-19 (ME ​= ​0.146, CI ​= ​0.049, 0.244), being very worried for oneself (ME ​= ​0.181, CI ​= ​0.093, 0.269) and for relatives and friends (ME ​= ​0.150, CI ​= ​0.065, 0.235), being unable to obtain medical care (ME ​= ​0.126, CI ​= ​0.033, 0.220), losing household income (ME ​= ​0.123, CI ​= ​0.033, 0.214), and not having enough to eat (ME ​= ​0.118, CI ​= ​0.008, 0.228). Five exposures were significantly associated with the probability of elevated PD: COVID-related worry for oneself (ME ​= ​0.231, CI ​= ​0.143, 0.319) and for relatives and friends (ME ​= ​0.212, CI ​= ​0.131, 0.293), two medical stressors (could not access medical care ME ​= ​0.111, CI ​= ​0.013, 0.208; household member had unmet medical needs ME ​= ​0.118, CI ​= ​0.005, 0.231), and not having enough to eat (ME ​= ​0.135, CI ​= ​0.018, 0.251).

*Fig. 2: Marginal effects and 95% confidence intervals from adjusted logistic regression models of elevated PTS and PD symptoms at F4 on pandemic-related exposures. Figure presents marginal effects from 14 separate logistic regression models of elevated pandemic-related PTS and of elevated PD, one for each pandemic-related exposure (N = 424). Models adjusted for F4 survey month, age, race/ethnicity, marital status, number of children, prior income and social support, prior mental and physical health, current physical health conditions, and exposure to Hurricane Katrina. Solid black markers indicate statistically significant marginal effects (p ​< ​.05). F4 = Follow-up 4; HH = Household; PD = Psychological distress; PTS = Posttraumatic stress.*

Table 2 presents full results from models of elevated pandemic-related PTS and PD at F4 on the pandemic-related exposure index. Each additional exposure was associated with 23% higher odds of elevated PTS (OR ​= ​1.23, CI ​= ​1.13, 1.35) and 19% higher odds of elevated PD (OR ​= ​1.19, CI ​= ​1.09, 1.30). In terms of marginal effects, an additional pandemic-related exposure was associated with a 4.2-percentage-point increase in the probability of elevated pandemic-related PTS (ME ​= ​0.042, CI ​= ​0.026, 0.058), and a 3.6-percentage-point increase in the probability of elevated PD (ME ​= ​0.036, CI ​= ​0.018, 0.053), on average. Only two covariates demonstrated significant associations with both measures of mental health adversity in these and other models: poorer pre-pandemic mental health (PD at F3) and higher exposure to Hurricane Katrina.

## Discussion

This study compared the prevalence, presentation, and predictors of mental health adversity during the COVID-19 pandemic to those following another mass crisis within a single sample, contributing to the disaster mental health literature in three ways. First, our results suggest that mental health adversity was as or more prevalent during the pandemic as it was following Hurricane Katrina, one of the deadliest, costliest weather-related disasters in modern U.S. history. Using longitudinal survey data from low-income mothers affected by both events, we found that the prevalence of elevated PTS was strikingly similar 1-year into the pandemic (41.6%) as 1-year post-Katrina (41.9%), while the prevalence of elevated PD was dramatically higher during the pandemic (48.3% versus 37.2%). Like Hurricane Katrina, and against some predictions (Ng et al., 2020), the COVID-19 pandemic appears to have prompted symptoms of both PTS and PD.

Second, our results suggest that mass crises of various typologies imperil mental health through exposure to potentially traumatic or stressful experiences. We found that experiencing the death of a loved one due to COVID-19, being very worried about one’s health and that of relatives and friends, and delaying or forgoing medical care during the pandemic were associated with poor mental health. A previous study of these data likewise identified bereavement, fear or worry, and disrupted medical care as salient predictors of mental health adversity following Hurricane Katrina (Raker et al., 2020). Economic stressors, which were not assessed previously (Raker et al., 2020), were also associated with pandemic-related PTS symptoms in the current study. Our findings echo those of earlier research showing stressor exposure to be associated with mental health challenges during the pandemic (Ettman et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021). Unfortunately, the exposures we identified as salient were common during the pandemic, particularly among racialized minorities and low-income populations (Cooper and Williams, 2020; Czeisler, 2020; Perry et al., 2021).

Notably, several exposures that were associated with pandemic-related PTS may not be considered traumatic by current guidelines (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), including fear or worry, unemployment, and reduced or insufficient income. These findings could be interpreted as aligned with calls to expand formal definitions of trauma and PTS disorder. Indeed, longstanding debates regarding “what counts” as traumatic and which experiences can prompt the development of PTS disorder have resurfaced during the pandemic (Horesh and Brown, 2020; McNally, 2003; Norrholm et al., 2021). That said, these exposures may have proxied for traumatic experiences that were not assessed in the current study, such as domestic violence. Future research should more thoroughly investigate the phenomenology of PTS symptoms following mass crises to shed further light on this issue.

Finally, findings from the current study underscore that mental health during times of crisis relates not only to contemporaneous experiences, but also to prior psychological vulnerability and previous traumatic or stressful exposures. Consistent with prior work (Goldmann and Galea, 2014), we found that pre-pandemic mental health and exposure to Hurricane Katrina were independently associated with PTS and PD symptoms during the pandemic. These results are relevant to growing concerns over the consequences of repeated disaster exposure, which may have long-term and cumulative effects on mental health (Leppold et al., 2022).

This study has several limitations. First, results may not generalize nationally, as our sample comprised primarily Black mothers who were originally low-income students in New Orleans. The sociodemographic homogeneity of our sample also precludes us from examining mental health disparities across racial/ethnic or socioeconomic subgroups. That said, our sample reflects a priority population for disaster planning and mitigation efforts, one that has been disproportionately impacted by the pandemic and prior disasters (Clouston et al., 2021; Cooper and Williams, 2020; Goldmann and Galea, 2014). Second, while longitudinal data from individuals exposed to two distinct crises simplifies the comparison of mental health outcomes in some ways (e.g., by holding constant sociodemographic factors and measurement), this strategy does have weaknesses. Respondents were 15 years older during the pandemic than they were during Hurricane Katrina, and their resources and responsibilities may have changed over time in ways that affected their mental health. That our sample was restricted to Hurricane Katrina survivors also raises questions regarding generalizability. Indeed, results suggest that experiences during Hurricane Katrina influenced mental health responses to the pandemic. We invite future researchers to further explore how mental health reactions to crisis depend on life course stage and prior exposure to trauma and stress, including other mass emergencies. Third, while we assessed 14 separate pandemic-related exposures reflecting personal experience with the virus, fear or worry, and impacts on healthcare, childcare, and household finances, these measures do not cover the full range of stressful pandemic-related experiences. Relatedly, while our additive index of pandemic-related exposures allows for comparisons to other studies (Ettman et al., 2020; Raker et al., 2020), it comes with the tradeoff of imposing uniform weighting of each exposure. Future work would benefit from interrogating additional exposures, such as essential worker status and social isolation, and other types of indices, such as those constructed using principal component analysis. Fourth, with two dependent variables, 14 pandemic-related exposures, and an index, we estimated 30 associations of interest applying standard significance thresholds (p ​< ​.05). Imposing Bonferroni adjustments for multiple comparisons would result in a markedly more conservative significance threshold (p ​< ​.002), rendering many associations non-significant.

Our findings underscore the need for expanded and continued access to mental health services that are sensitive to various symptoms, including those of PTS, as the pandemic recedes. Furthermore, by conceptualizing pandemics as a form of mass crisis, this study illuminates experiences that may heighten risk for mental health adversity across contexts. People experiencing bereavement, fear or worry, complications accessing medical care, or economic stressors in a disaster setting may be particularly vulnerable to mental health challenges, as are those who have experienced psychopathology or been exposed to disasters previously. These conclusions are based on findings across two distinct crises: a drawn-out global pandemic and an acute, localized weather-related disaster. They should therefore inform responses to future mass crises, regardless of typology, to prevent and address secondary impacts on mental health.
